la:verb:sopio.html:
sōpio, īvi or ĭi, ītum, 4, v. a.
sopor
,
to deprive of feeling or sense; esp. by sleep, to put or lull to sleep.
Lit. (class.; most freq. in part. perf.; in Cic. only so; cf. sedo): impactus ita est saxo, ut sopiretur, became unconscious or senseless, was stunned, ; ; : vino oneratos sopire,; fin.; ; ; .—In part. perf.: castoreo gravi mulier sopita recumbit, Lucr b, 794; so, sopitum vulnere ac nihil sentientem,: quem vigilantem sic eluseritis, sopitum oportet fallatis,: delphinus sopitus odoris novitate,: ut sopito corpore ipse (animus) vigilet,; : hostes,; (opp. vigiles); 31, 23; ; ; ; ; : sensus,; : sopitae quietis tempus, of deep or sound sleep, .—
In the poets, pregn., to lay to rest, i. e. to kill: aliquem fundā,.—Pass., to be laid to rest, to die: (Homerus) sceptra potitus, eādem aliis sopitu' quiete est,; cf. .—
Transf., of things concr. and abstr., to lull to sleep, set, or lay at rest; to calm, settle, still, quiet: venti sopiuntur,: sopito mari,: sopitos suscitat ignes,; ; cf.: aras excitat,: draconis saevi sopivi impetum, Enn. ap. P. (Trag. v. 314 Vahl.): haec omnia veteris imperatoris maturitas

brevi sopiit ac sustulit, .—Part. perf.: quibus (blandimentis) sopita virtus coniveret,lulled to sleep,: munera militiaï,: furor armorum ubique,: ingenium pecudis,: gloria vitiis,, ext. 1: artes,.

la:noun:sopor.html:
sŏpor, ōris, m.
Sanscr. root svap-, sleep; cf. somnus; Gr. ὕπνος
,
a deep sleep.
Lit., in gen., sleep (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose; not in Cic.; cf. somnus): lucrum praeposivi sopori et quieti,: cum eum cibo vinoque gravatum sopor oppressisset,: sopore discusso,; ; ; 8, 6, 26; but also opp. somnus: hujus (junci) semine somnum allici, sed modum servandum, ne sopor fiat,: sopore placans artus languidos, Att. ap. : cum suavi devinxit membra sopore Somnus,; ; : nox erat et placidum carpebant fessa soporem Corpora,: piger his labante languore oculos sopor operit,: fessos sopor inrigat artus,: placidum petivit soporem,: occupet ut fessi lumina victa sopor,. —Personified, Sopor = Somnus, ; ; . —In plur., (Müll. sapores).—
Pregn., the sleep of death, death: in soporem conlocastis nudos,; : aeternus,: perpetuus,.—
Transf.
Stupefaction, lethargy, stupor: neque dormire excitatus, neque vigilare ebrius poterat, sed semisomno sopore ... jactabatur, Cael. ap. : temulento sopore profligatus,. —
Drowsiness, laziness, indifference: sopor et ignavia,; .—
Poppy-juice, opium: e nigro papavere sopor gignitur scapo inciso,.—
A sleepingdraught, sleeping - potion: sopore sumpto dormiturus,; so (opp. venenum) ; ; .—
The temple (of the head; cf. Germ. Schläfe): laevus,.

la:verb:soporo.html:
sŏpōro, no
perf., ātum, 1, v. a.
sopor
, to put or lay asleep, cast into sleep; to deprive of sense or feeling, to stupefy (not ante-Aug.; usu. in part. perf.).
Lit.: si saepius expergiscitur aliquis quam assuevit, deinde iterum soporatur,falls asleep,: opium mentem soporat sensusque abalienat,: serpentes soporari,: ut soporetur illa sopore enecans vis earum,.—In part. perf.: soporatos hostes,: aquatilia quiete placida ceu soporata,: soporatos artus premit alta quies,: vellera,; .—
Transf., with an inanim. or abstr. object, to lay at rest, to still, quiet, allay (syn. sopire): multo Imbre rogum,: soporatus dolor,.—
To render soporific: ramus Vi soporatus Stygia,; ; .

la:other:Sophocles.gloss: Sophocles of Colonus, a celebrated Greek dramatic poet (ca. 497 BCE – 405 BCE); Sophocles was one of the three greatest Greek tragedians. In the Athenian dramatic competitions of the Festival of Dionysus, he won more first prizes (around 20) than any other playwright, and placed second in all others he participated in. He is best remembered for his Oedipus Cycle of plays.
